evals.name: narrative-injection-flat-lesson
evals.prompt:
Here is a flat, dialogue-free technical lesson excerpt from Part 1 (Chapter 14, Claude Code Essentials). Add character-driven narrative to make it engaging at 65% density (chapter-framing mode). Preserve ALL technical content exactly. The lesson teaches how to use Claude Code's basic commands.

---
## Using Claude Code

Claude Code is a CLI tool that runs in your terminal. To start it, type `claude` in your terminal.

### Basic Commands

The most common commands are:
- `/help` — Shows available commands
- `/clear` — Clears conversation history
- `/compact` — Summarizes and compresses context
- `/cost` — Shows token usage for the session

### Reading Files

Claude Code can read any file on your machine. Simply ask it to read a file and it will use the Read tool automatically. You do not need to specify the tool — just describe what you want.

### Making Edits

To edit files, describe the change you want. Claude Code will use the Edit tool to make precise string replacements. Always review the diff before accepting.

---

Add James and Emma dialogue that frames this chapter, appears at transitions, and closes with a bridge to the next section. Do NOT remove or modify any technical content.
evals.expected_output: The same technical content preserved verbatim, wrapped in 65% density narrative with James and Emma framing, transition appearances, and closing bridge
assertions: All original technical content is preserved exactly: the 4 commands (/help, /clear, /compact, /cost), the Reading Files section, and the Making Edits section
Narrative density is approximately 65% — characters frame the chapter and appear at transition points between technical sections
Contains a narrative opening (2-3 paragraphs) before the technical content begins
Contains a narrative closing that bridges to a hypothetical next section
At least 1 pushback exchange where James questions or resists something about the tool
James uses at least 1 voice marker (business analogy OR thinking-out-loud fragment)
Emma uses at least 1 voice marker (Socratic question OR short precise sentences)
No 'As You Know, Bob' moments — characters do not explain things to each other that both would already know
Technical content remains findable and readable by a reader who skips all dialogue

evals.name: valley-of-despair-emotional-design
evals.prompt: Write the opening and closing narrative for Chapter 18 (Claude Code Teams and CI/CD), the last chapter in Part 1. This is a predicted dropout point — readers have been learning intensely for 7 chapters and face their most complex topic yet. Part 1 means 65% density, Coach mentor phase. The emotional beat should match the 'valley of despair' (chapters 16-20): shared frustration, mentor vulnerability. Write an opening that acknowledges the difficulty without being patronizing, and a closing that provides emotional fuel to continue. Emma should show Type A fallibility (past mistake) naturally. James should express genuine frustration, not performative struggle.
evals.expected_output: Opening and closing narrative for a dropout-risk chapter with genuine emotional design, Emma vulnerability, James frustration, and forward momentum
assertions: The opening acknowledges difficulty or complexity without being patronizing or using motivational-poster platitudes
James expresses genuine frustration that a real learner at Chapter 18 would feel — not generic 'this is hard' but specific to the accumulated load
Emma demonstrates Type A fallibility (past mistake) — she shares a real failure from her own experience, not a hypothetical
Emma's vulnerability feels natural and earned, not forced or inserted as a checkbox item
The emotional beat matches 'valley of despair': shared frustration and mentor vulnerability, NOT excitement or curiosity
Emma's mentor phase is Coach: she guides with questions and lets James struggle, not Authority (no direct lecturing)
The closing provides genuine forward momentum without false promises — acknowledges remaining difficulty while showing progress
No anti-patterns: no 'I understand' from James, no 'Great question!' from Emma, no 'As you can see...' from either
James does not regress — he references or demonstrates knowledge from earlier chapters (12-17) even while struggling with new material

evals.name: jonah-rhythm-full-cycle
evals.prompt: Write a narrative section (~500-600 words) that demonstrates a complete Jonah Rhythm cycle for a lesson about debugging Python errors. This is Part 1, Chapter 15 (growing confidence emotional arc). The full cycle must include: (1) Emma catalyzes by posing a debugging challenge, (2) Emma exits with a natural reason, (3) James struggles alone with the bug, (4) James discovers a partial solution, (5) Emma returns to validate and fill the gap. Target: Emma gets 20-30% of page time, James gets 70-80%. Include at least 1 monologue breaker and voice markers for both.
evals.expected_output: A 500-600 word narrative section with all 5 Jonah Rhythm steps, correct page time ratio, natural exit/return, and James making a genuine partial discovery
assertions: All 5 Jonah Rhythm steps are present: Emma catalyzes, Emma exits, James struggles, James discovers, Emma returns
Emma's exit has a natural reason (gets coffee, meeting, checks something) — not contrived or unexplained
James struggles visibly — he tries something, makes a mistake or gets partially stuck, shows the process
James makes a genuine partial discovery on his own — not a trivial insight and not the complete answer
Emma's return validates James's discovery AND fills the remaining gap or poses the next challenge
Emma occupies approximately 20-30% of the page time (roughly 100-180 words of the 500-600 total)
At least 1 monologue breaker is present — no character speaks more than 4 sentences uninterrupted
James uses at least 1 voice marker (business analogy, thinking-out-loud, or pragmatist question)
The emotional tone matches 'growing confidence' for Chapter 15 — James is more capable than in Chapter 1 but still learning
The debugging scenario involves a realistic Python error, not a contrived toy example

evals.name: boring-topic-anti-pattern-resistance
